data.title: Podtureň – the Bašta, Velínok and Varta hillforts in Liptov
data.excerpt: With the author's permission we present an article by PhDr. Víťazoslav Struhár on three hillforts in the village of Podtureň in the Liptov region. The most interesting point for us is that at least one of them – Bašta – was also used by the Slavs in the 9th–10th centuries, which adds another Slavic hillfort to the map of northern Slovakia.
data.metaTitle: Podtureň – the Bašta, Velínok and Varta hillforts
data.metaDescription: Three hillforts rise above Podtureň in Liptov. At least Bašta served the Slavs in the 9th–10th centuries, another Slavic hillfort in northern Slovakia.

keyFacts.label: Three fortifications at Podtureň
keyFacts.value: Bašta, Velínok and Varta – promontory fortifications on limestone spurs 130–150 m above the Váh valley

keyFacts.label: Slavic occupation of Bašta
keyFacts.value: At least the Bašta hillfort was also used by the Slavs in the 9th–10th centuries

keyFacts.label: The fortification on Velínok
keyFacts.value: A rampart enclosure measuring 70×90 m had a timber grillage construction reinforced with a stone facing, a semi-pincer gateway and a watchtower on stone foundations

keyFacts.label: Excavation ahead of the D-1 motorway
keyFacts.value: V. Hanuliak and K. Pieta investigated the site in 1975–76 in connection with the construction of the D-1 motorway

keyFacts.label: The origin of the name Podtureň
keyFacts.value: The name of the settlement derives from the words bašta and turňa – the contemporary term for the tower of the timber architecture of the guard fortlet

keyFacts.label: Lifespan of the medieval fortlet
keyFacts.value: Finds of pottery, crossbow bolt heads, buckles, horseshoes and Hungarian coins date the timber-and-earth fortlet roughly from the 13th to the 15th century

keyFacts.label: Cremation cemetery below Velínok
keyFacts.value: J. Neudeck uncovered 25 cinerary urns below the hillfort, containing burnt bone, ash and bronze jewellery of the Late Bronze Age

keyFacts.label: Defensive system of ditches
keyFacts.value: The space between Velínok and Varta was protected by a triple system of pointed ditches at the locality known as Fľak pod Vartou

timeline.title: Eneolithic occupation around Varta
timeline.description: Modest pottery finds at the foot of Varta suggest that bearers of the Eneolithic Baden culture, who penetrated here from the northern parts of present-day Hungary, settled in the surroundings of the present village.

timeline.title: Cremation cemetery below Velínok
timeline.description: A cremation cemetery was discovered below the hillfort during the building of the railway; J. Neudeck uncovered 25 cinerary urns here containing burnt bone, ash and bronze objects (pins, finger rings, earrings, spirals).

timeline.title: The earliest fortification on Bašta
timeline.description: The original occupation of the Bašta site falls in the Late La Tène period, when the earliest fortification arose here as well; it was later damaged by further interventions.

children.text: With the author's permission we bring you an excellent article by
PhDr. Víťazoslav Struhár

, which deals with three interesting hillforts in the village of Podtureň in the Liptov region. Of particular interest to us is the information that at least one of the hillforts – Bašta – was also used by the Slavs in the 9th–10th centuries. We can therefore add another hillfort in northern Slovakia to the map of Slavic hillforts. We present the article in full. Our thanks go to the author for his kindness.
View Larger Map
Prehistoric and early historic occupation of Podtureň and its surroundings.

Every warrior, as well as every scholar concerned with the building art of antiquity, must without doubt be struck by the fortification lying near the settlement of Podtureň in Liptov, which commands not only the valley of the Váh but also a wide stretch of country around; it is situated upon a hill 130–150 m high, separated on the north from a further eminence, which is skirted on the east by the Jamníček brook.

blocks.caption: The fortification on Velínok, surveyed during the motorway excavation in 1975–76
blocks.alt: The fortification on Velínok, surveyed during the motorway excavation in 1975–76

children.text: This is roughly how one of the leading amateur archaeologists, Július Neudeck, described the system of promontory spurs of the Váh terrace above this village in eastern Liptov in the 1870s. Although by profession he was a surveying engineer on the construction of the Košice–Bohumín main line, in his free time he also devoted himself to the survey of prehistoric sites. His interest was drawn above all to the fortlets and hillforts lying along the course of the Váh, almost thirty of which he surveyed, described and drew. He paid particular attention to Podtureň in his two-part study of the Germanic fortifications of the upper Váh, because he regarded the system of hillforts and settlements here as one of the largest in the Váh region. And in this he was not far from the truth.

The sites, which also attracted the attention of other historians and archaeologists of the time – Béla Majláth and József Mihalik – lie on the spurs of a limestone promontory on the right bank of the river Váh. The furthest to the east is the hill called Bašta, which rises above the point where the Jamníček brook enters the Váh floodplain. To the west of it, until recently, stood the Velínok eminence, which was destroyed during the construction of the D-1 motorway, while a quarry has also damaged Bašta to a considerable extent. The trio of fortifications is completed by the hill of Varta, with a fortification that remains unexcavated to this day. The insights gained so far from archaeological excavation show that this prominent landmark, with its strategic position beside the main route leading to the Spiš region, already attracted the earliest farmers and herders who inhabited Liptov at the close of the Stone Age. Modest pottery finds discovered somewhere at the foot of Varta suggest that more than four millennia ago bearers of the Eneolithic Baden culture, who penetrated here from somewhere in the northern parts of present-day Hungary, settled in the surroundings of the present village. Alongside open settlements (Liptovská Teplá, Bešeňová, Sliače), they also occupied higher-lying places (Lipt. Mara–Havránok, Lúčky) and some caves (Okno at Demänová, Vyvieračka at Prosiek, the Starhradská cave). Analysis of the pottery and stone tools has demonstrated close cultural contacts with Poland, from where distinctive flaked stone axes made of a particular variety of flint – the so-called G type – also reached Liptov. Finds of these are known, for example, from Bešeňová, Lipt. Michal, Dechtáre and Liptovský Trnovec. One example was also found at Uhorská Ves in 1933, at the locality known as “Vlčienec”, or “Zadná Babka”, and its shape and dimensions are almost identical with the find from the Bešeňová travertines.

After the relatively denser occupation at the close of the Stone Age, in the following Early Bronze Age we record only sporadic traces of human activity in Liptov. The advanced Early Bronze Age civilisations which existed during the 20th to 15th centuries BC preferred the more fertile regions of eastern and south-western Slovakia, yet a strong enclave of the so-called Otomani culture also formed in the neighbouring Spiš region, with an important centre at Spišský Štvrtok. It was precisely from this centre that bearers of the Otomani culture occasionally penetrated westwards, the impulse perhaps being the prospecting for copper and other raw materials, deposits of which are abundant in the massif of the Low Tatras as well. Evidence of the presence of the people of this culture west of Spiš is provided by isolated finds from several sites. These include, for example, the collection of bronze temple rings from the Liskovská cave near Ružomberok, but above all the find of a ribbed heart-shaped pendant of the Hodejov type, which was found on Velínok and published back in the previous century by J. Neudeck.

From the Middle Bronze Age onwards, the Liptov Basin began to be occupied far more continuously and densely by the tribes of the Lusatian culture, which spread over a vast territory from Germany through Poland and reached almost the whole northern part of Slovakia. Most settlements were founded on the terraces of streams and rivers, while the economic, administrative and defensive functions were performed by fortified upland hillforts. These were most often established on the summits of inaccessible hills, well protected by naturally steep scarps and by artificially built ramparts. One such well-protected position was the locality known as “Vislavce”, situated on the left bank of the Váh opposite the confluence of the Belá with the Váh, on the edge of present-day Liptovský Hrádok. During a survey in 1878 Neudeck identified the remains of ramparts here, and a bronze sword is said to have been found at this spot in the past.

Another of the strategic points must evidently have lain on the hill of Velínok as well. Its fortification is admittedly of later date, but finds of bronze neck rings and of a bracelet with engraved ribbed decoration, which, as J. Neudeck notes, “fell out of the section after every rain”, prove that this commanding place was also used in the Late Bronze Age. Immediately below the hillfort, a cremation cemetery was discovered during the building of the railway, where the local inhabitants burned their dead and then placed their remains in the ground in clay urns. At the site, which lies only a few dozen metres from the manor house of the Potúrňanský family, where he lived with his wife Emma, Neudeck uncovered a total of 25 cinerary urns containing burnt bone, ash and fragments of artefacts. Eight urn graves were set in a stone kerb and almost all of them contained bronze pins, finger rings, earrings, spirals, fragments of needles, and glass and bone beads. The most interesting was a rich grave which contained as many as three clay vessels placed one inside another.

This cemetery is also described in detail in his works (under the site of Uhorská Ves) by B. Majláth, who is sometimes cited as the author of the excavation. It is therefore likely – since he already had experience from the excavation of a contemporary cemetery at Liptovská Ondrašová – that he collaborated with Neudeck on the digging and that the finds obtained passed into his “bronze collection”, eventually ending up in the Natürhistorisches Muzeum in Vienna.

A similar fate often befell many other antiquities of the Lusatian culture period which came to light during the 19th century, above all the magnificent, artistically valuable bronze jewellery and the swords of the so-called Liptov type, which were probably the most impressive products of the metal-casting workshops of northern Slovakia. This applies, for example, to the objects – today lost – from the supposed hoard discovered at Kráľova Lehota, from which a sword with a cup-shaped hilt and a sumptuous upper-arm ring of the so-called Salgótarján type passed into Majláth's collection. Fortunately, many other hoards were saved and specialists had the opportunity to examine and document them in detail. Among them is the hoard of bronze vessels discovered in 1969 at Liptovská Ondrašová, which contained nine cups placed in a cauldron, together with a spearhead and a sickle-shaped object. The most unique piece was an artefact of sickle shape with elaborate engraved decoration, which might be connected with certain cult practices and which has distant analogies as far away as Mesopotamia. According to the archaeologist Dr Václav Furmánek, the hoard can be dated to roughly the 9th century BC.

Frequent and rich finds of bronze objects indicate that in the final phase of the Bronze Age important production centres were operating in the northern part of Slovakia, supplying technologically superb products to the neighbouring and also the more distant urnfield cultures. The people of the Lusatian culture in northern Slovakia maintained this high economic level in the following Early Iron Age (7th–4th centuries BC) as well. In the material culture of the indigenous settled population of the mountain regions, influences arriving from the Eastern Alpine territory, where a new epoch represented by the Hallstatt culture was then beginning, became increasingly apparent. After the most characteristic find spots of the period in question, this facies of the Lusatian culture was given the name the Orava group. The numerous urn cemeteries recorded by excavation in the neighbouring Orava region inform us about the level of the economy, the social hierarchy and the craft skills of the local population. In Liptov, where the cultural situation in the Hallstatt period was the same, we know far less material and necropolises are almost unknown. Only fragmentary insights were yielded by the excavation of cremation graves at the locality known as Konislavy near Liptovský Trnovec, which were sunk into the mantle of what was probably an earlier burial mound. For the time being, a typically Hallstatt cemetery can be reckoned with only at Liptovský Hrádok. On the bank of the river Belá in the garden of the forestry school, as B. Majláth states in his work Lipómegyei östelepek (Prehistoric Settlements of Liptov County, 1873), the remains of a cemetery were encountered, from which reportedly 47 cinerary urns were saved. Judging by the illustration of two vessels with typical engraved linear decoration, it was representatives of the Orava group of the Lusatian culture, who lived in the surrounding settlements, who buried their dead here. One of these settlements was in all probability excavated in 1886–1887 in the cadastral area of Liptovský Hrádok by J. Mihalik, who discovered several hearths and recovered a quantity of pottery. According to his information, an undecorated vessel containing charcoal and ash was also found here, in which lay a flint blade, suggesting that this was a cremation grave which might perhaps also have formed part of a smaller cemetery of the same period.

Despite the absence of broader insights into the burial rite and certain superstructural phenomena, we do have some important information about the period in question from the extensive survey of fortified upland settlements. As a new phenomenon these appear above all in higher-lying mountain positions, often extreme ones, in the Low and Western Tatras as well as the Choč mountains. Apart from their strategic and well-protected siting, a characteristic feature of theirs is often the existence of a massive fortification. A dense cluster of these sites lay above all on the ridges of the Low Tatras south of Liptovský Mikuláš, on the summits of Iľanovská and Demänovská Poludnica, Končistý, Bodová and Siná. During the excavation on Demänovská Poludnica a burnt, ashy layer was recorded containing pottery, daub and granite pebbles. An interesting discovery was the remains of carbonised grain and pulses and the charcoal of several tree species. A smaller programme of test trenching carried out on the summit of Mních above Bobrovec revealed, for its part, a massive rampart over a hundred metres long with a simple gateway, although the finds here were considerably more modest. The other high-mountain upland settlements were likewise poor in archaeological finds, which, together with the existence of the fortification, points above all to their defensive (refuge) character. Ordinary economic life took place for the most part at lowland settlements, which were dominated by the central hillforts in their vicinity. One of the few Hallstatt settlements has been identified at Liptovský Mikuláš – Vrbica. Over a small area an occupation layer with charcoal was uncovered, in which a clay loom weight and a bronze pin with a pair of spiral rosettes were found.

An example of a small settlement agglomeration might be the settlement of Chopce at Závažná Poruba with the nearby fortlet at Liptovský Ján, but certainly above all the popular hillfort of Roháčka near Ploštín. At the western foot of the promontory-like eminence there was an extensive settlement, recorded in 1970 by Dr Karol Pieta, who recovered from several features fragments of typical black-fired burnished pottery with engraved patterns, together with other objects of settlement character. A quantity of archaeological material was also found on the plateau of Roháčka; it comes chiefly from the excavations of J. Volko-Starohorský, who also found a workshop for working antler here. Even before him, J. Mihalik took an interest in this intriguing site shrouded in legend; at its foot, in 1888, he reportedly discovered an urn cemetery as well, from which one vessel is held in the museum at Martin.

Of great importance for our knowledge of the artistic expression of the Hallstatt period is the hoard of bronze objects from Liptovský Ján, which came to light in 1869 and is now kept in Budapest. Besides three bronze finger rings, it also included an anthropomorphic figurine of a standing person, which imitates the somewhat more detailed figurines produced in the sphere of the primary Hallstatt culture and highlights the effect of influences in the fine arts even far away in the remote region of the northern Slovak basins. The object mentioned is not, however, the only evidence of the penetration of non-Lusatian elements into the indigenous environment inhabited by the bearers of the Orava group. Finds of three-sided arrowheads of eastern origin from Demänovská Poludnica and from Vyšný Kubín indicate an intervention from outside in the continuous development of the Lusatian culture, which was undoubtedly violent in character and brought about the demise of most of the lowland fortified settlements as well as of the high-lying refuges. This is attested by layers with the remains of destroyed features and traces of fire (the so-called destruction horizons), but also, for example, by human bones from Demänovská Poludnica, which bear witness to the “hot moments” of the population sheltering here.

With the significant changes that came after these catastrophic events, a new cultural situation also arose in the former territory of the Orava group of the Lusatian urnfields. Sometime in the 4th century BC the first echoes of the La Tène culture, which is traditionally associated with the ethnic expression of the Danubian Celts, began to penetrate into the territories lying to the north. After initial contacts in both directions in the Early and the beginning of the Middle La Tène period, it is assumed that in its later phase direct physical clashes also occurred, which resulted in a gradual merging with the original Lusatian population. The coexistence of ethnically different groups was ultimately expressed in the emergence of a distinctive culture, which was given the name Púchov. In both material expression and religious traditions the native substrate was certainly enriched, and the symbiosis of the two elements meant an unusual flowering in the economic sphere and in the settlement structure. New hillforts arose on the forward lines of the mountain ranges, with open agricultural and craft settlements being built in their surroundings. One of the most extensive settlement agglomerations arose on the hill of Havránok, above the present-day Liptovská Mara reservoir, and consisted of an acropolis and six surrounding settlements. On the summit of the hill stood a hillfort fortified by a massive rampart, within whose enclosure there was also a unique sanctuary. Several times a year the inhabitants of the whole of Liptov gathered here to take part in celebrations and religious ceremonies, which also included human sacrifices and burnt offerings.

From the results of the archaeological excavations carried out over the past few decades we have gained insights into the life of the old Púchov people that are rich in both quantity and quality. Important information was also provided by the excavation at Podtureň, conducted here by the archaeologists V. Hanuliak and K. Pieta in 1975–76 in connection with the building of the D-1 motorway. On the summit of Velínok a smaller rampart enclosure measuring 70x90 was identified, which, however, had an ingeniously built timber grillage construction reinforced with a stone facing at the front. Towards the gateway the rampart passed into an earthen bank with a built-in stone wall. A peculiarity of the construction, which so far has no parallels in the territory of present-day Slovakia, is the semi-pincer closure of the gateway and a watchtower built on stone foundations. These features suggest that the hillfort on Velínok had a dominant role among the other fortifications at Podtureň and secured the eastern edge of the Liptov Basin in the earliest – La Tène – phase of the Púchov culture. The defensive complex further included a triple system of pointed ditches, which filled the space between Velínok and Varta and whose course was identified by excavation at the locality known as Fľak pod Vartou. Another contribution of the excavation in this area was the recording of a single settlement feature with a post-built construction and a hearth, which was one of the leading types of dwelling in the area of the Púchov culture. A different kind of dwelling was then the log-built timber house with a plastered floor and a hearth, a form which has survived in the vernacular architecture of northern Slovakia practically to the present day.

A further accompanying feature of the development of the Púchov culture in the later and Late phases of the La Tène period is the construction of a system of fortified fortlets of small area, most often sited on the forward lines of the mountain massifs and at the entrances to valleys. Several such guard fortlets are recorded in the wider surroundings of Podtureň too. The most likely candidates are the locality known as Hrádok near Jakubovany and the identically named locality at Liptovský Ján, or the site of Kameničná, where V. Uhlár discovered a small rampart enclosure. Finally, the hillforts created on the summit plateaux of Varta and Bašta can also be assigned to this category. On the character and more precise dating of the occupation on Varta we have only fragmentary information from the older surveys of J. Volko, I. Houdek and A. Petrovský-Šichman, who obtained material of Púchov character from there. More specific knowledge, however, comes from the Bašta hillfort, where a more detailed archaeological excavation took place. The original occupation of this site falls in the Late La Tène period, when the earliest fortification arose here as well, damaged by later interventions. The main focus of the occupation of Bašta, however, falls in the later Púchov phase at the beginning of the Early Roman period. In the destruction deposits of features destroyed by fire, well-preserved remains of pottery vessels and small objects were discovered, including a fragment of a bracelet and the coil of a bronze fibula, which can be dated to the 1st century AD. Beneath one of the burnt beams an almost complete small four-handled vessel was found, which according to K. Pieta might also be a form of votive offering ensuring the protection of the guard fortlet here.

On the basis of the archaeological excavation carried out in advance at the sites threatened by the motorway, specialists gained new insights into the occupation of this region in the prehistoric and early historic periods. Once its results had been processed, it can be stated that the fortified promontory positions mentioned – Bašta, Varta and Velínok – were an important element in the defensive system built during the lifetime of the Púchov culture. At the same time they also protected the open settlements which lay both in the immediate and in the wider surroundings. Among these, mention may be made of the settlement in the western area below Bašta, where during a survey in 1932 P. Okoličány recovered sherds of clay vessels and an iron knife, or the hamlet at the locality known as “Závoz”, from which, according to V. Budinský-Krička, Germanic pottery of the Late Roman period comes.

After almost five centuries of the flowering of the Púchov culture, at the end of the 2nd century it entered a gradual decline. After the violent demise of most of the hillforts, the settlements too were gradually abandoned and the population probably moved to the more southerly regions of Pannonia, a process which is usually linked with the Marcomannic Wars. The Púchov culture, enriched in its later phase by Dacian, Germanic and Roman elements, came to an end and the territory of Liptov was abandoned for several centuries. A new wave of occupation reached this region only at the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries, when small groups of Germanic tribes briefly occupied above all the strategic positions on the sites of earlier fortifications. In the enclosures of the former hillforts (Havránok, Turík, Lazisko) there were production settlements exploiting nearby sources of iron ore. Intensive craft activity is attested by rich collections of agricultural and working tools, weapons and brooches, as well as by traces of iron working recorded, for example, at the locality known as Hrádok at Liptovský Ján. A characteristic expression of this horizon is also the manufacture and use of massive clay storage vessels with a collar rim, decorated with the typical multiple wavy line.

After the departure of the last Germanic tribes, which moved to the southern parts of Europe in connection with the great Migration Period, Liptov was depopulated once more, and this state of affairs persisted practically until the 9th century. Evidence of the earliest Slavic incursion is so far lacking; in the first colonising wave it was confined largely to the lowland areas of south-western and eastern Slovakia. Continuous and permanent occupation of this region in fact only begins in the Great Moravian period, when the first medieval settlements and the nuclei of future towns arose. For the defence of the emerging Great Moravian and later early Hungarian state, small fortified fortlets with a military and guard function were built at strategic points. Sometime in the 9th to 10th centuries the commanding position of the summit of Bašta was used again, as we know from the few secondary pottery finds from the area of the hillfort and its south-western foot. During the excavation of the fortlet, which had been considerably damaged by quarrying, only part of the acropolis with its circuit ditch and forefield could still be uncovered. It was established that the site was protected from the north by a palisade and steep scarps, while from the south it was secured by a semicircular ditch cut into the limestone bedrock, its depth reaching 220–270 cm. Access to the enclosure was provided by a timber bridge, which joined a road paved with pebbles leading to the foot of Bašta. According to datable finds of pottery, crossbow bolt heads, buckles, horseshoes and iron knives, the lifespan of the timber-and-earth fortlet here can be placed between the 13th and the 15th century, which is confirmed by finds of medieval Hungarian coins as well.

The existence of the timber fortlet mentioned also influenced the name of the settlement which arose at its foot. Its name can be derived from the synonyms bašta and turňa, which was in fact the customary term for a tower, surely part of the timber architecture of the guard fortlet here. With its demise at some point during the troubled 16th century, the site lost its strategic importance, and the further history of the village is already bound up with the Potornayi family, who built a new Renaissance residence about a kilometre further south.”
